(p-٣٧٩) Surat al-Hijr

It is Makki (revealed in Mecca) in its entirety, without any disagreement that we know of.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book﴾ has already been explained [Yunus: 1].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and a clear Qur'an﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions:

One of them: the Qur'an is the Book, and both names were combined for it.

The second: the Book is the Torah and the Gospel, and the Qur'an is our book. We have already mentioned the meaning of "clear" (mubin) at the beginning of Surat Yusuf.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "rubbama" with the letter ba' doubled (shaddah). Nafi', 'Asim and 'Abd al-Warith read "rubama" with the ba' unstressed (takhfif). Al-Farra' said: The Asad and Tamim tribes say "rubba" with the shaddah, while the people of the Hijaz and many of Qays say "rubba" with the lighter form. The Taym al-Rabab say "rabba" with a fatha on the ra'.

It was said: It was only read with the lighter form because of the doubling it contains, and doubled letters may be elided, as with "inna" and "lakinna," which they also lightened. Al-Zajjaj said: They say "rubba rajulin ja'ani" and "rubba rajulin ja'ani," and he recited:

Azuhayr, if the temples turn grey, then indeed
many a troop of mighty men have I enfolded with a troop.

This verse belongs to Abu Kabir al-Hudhali, and in his Diwan it reads:

Many a mighty troop have I enfolded with a troop.

The hay'al (هَيْضَل) is the plural of hay'alah, which is a group sent out to fight. He means: I enfolded them with their enemies in battle. "Rubba" is a word established for paucity, just as "kam" is for abundance. "Ma" was added after "rubba" so that a verb would follow it; you say "rubba rajulin ja'ani" and "rubbama ja'ani Zayd." Al-Akhfash said: "Ma" was added with "rubba" so that the verb after it would be spoken, and if you wish, you may make "ma" stand in the place of "shay'" (thing), as though you said "rubba shay'in," meaning "many a thing which those who disbelieved love." Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: "Ma" here carries the sense of "hin" (a time), so the meaning is: many a time they will wish.

The exegetes differed as to when this occurs for the disbelievers, on two views:

The first is that it is in the Hereafter. When is that? There are four opinions on it. The first: when the people of the Fire are gathered in the Fire, together with those of the People of the Qiblah whom God wills, the disbelievers say to the Muslims: "Were you not Muslims?" They say: "Yes." They say: "Then what has your Islam availed you, since you are with us in the Fire?" They say: "We had sins, and we were seized for them." God hears what they say, and commands that those of the People of the Qiblah in the Fire be brought out. When the disbelievers see this, they say: "Would that we had been Muslims, so that we might be brought out as they were brought out." This was related by Abu Musa al-Ash'ari from the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn 'Abbas held this in one narration, as did Anas ibn Malik, Mujahid, 'Ata', Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibrahim.

The second: God continues to show mercy and intercede until He says: "Whoever was a Muslim, let him enter Paradise." That is the time when those who disbelieved wish they had been Muslims. Mujahid related this from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: when the disbelievers witness the Resurrection, they wish they had been Muslims. Al-Zajjaj mentioned this.

The fourth: whenever the people of disbelief see one of the states of the Resurrection in which the disbeliever is punished and the believer is spared its harm, they wish for that. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this.

The second view: it is in this world, when they witness and the misguidance is made clear to them apart from guidance, and they know their final destination, they wish for that. This was said by al-Dahhak.

If it is said: When you say that "rubba" denotes paucity, and this verse is given as a threat, then what fits a threat is the magnification of what is threatened. To this there are three answers, which Ibn al-Anbari mentioned:

One: "Rubbama" applies both to paucity and to abundance, just as "al-nahil" (one who drinks) applies to the thirsty and the sated, and "al-jawn" applies to the black and the white.

The second: the terrors of the Resurrection and what befalls them of terrors are many upon them, so when their reason returns to them, they wish for that.

The third: if what they were warned of were something to be wished for in any single state of the torment, or if a person fears regret when it occurs and is not certain of it, it would still be obligatory for him to avoid it.

If it is said: How does the future tense come after "rubbama," when its usual pattern is that the past tense follows it? You say: "Rubbama laqitu 'Abd Allah" (Perhaps I met 'Abd Allah).

The answer: What God has promised is true, so its future is like its past. This is shown by His saying: ﴿And when God says: "O Jesus son of Mary"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], and His saying: ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out﴾ [al-A'raf: 44], and ﴿If you could see when they are terrified, then there will be no escape﴾ [Saba': 51]. Moreover, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' related from the Arabs that they say: "Rubbama yandamu fulan" (Perhaps so-and-so will regret), and a poet said:

Perhaps souls grow anxious over a matter,
and for it there is an opening like the untying of a knot.

Ibn al-Jawzi, Zad al-Masir, on Surah 15, verse 3:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope divert them﴾. That is: leave the disbelievers to take their share of this world, ﴿and let hope divert them﴾, that is: and let what they hope for in this world occupy them from taking their share of faith and obedience. ﴿But they will come to know﴾ when they arrive at the Resurrection the evil consequence of what they did. This is a warning and a threat. And this verse, according to the exegetes (mufassirun), is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 15, verses 4–5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not destroy any town﴾, meaning: We did not punish any of the people of a town (p-383) ﴿except that it had a known decree﴾, meaning: a fixed term that can be neither advanced nor delayed. ﴿No nation can precede its term, nor can they delay it.﴾ The "min" (مِن) here is extra (ṣila), and the meaning is: they cannot advance beyond the time decreed for them to reach, nor can they fall behind it. Al-Farra' (al-Farrāʾ) said: He said "ajalahā" (its term) because the word "umma" (nation) is feminine in form, and He said "yastakhirūna" (they delay) by reverting to its meaning as men (rijāl).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 15, verse 6–8:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are mad."﴾ Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The Reminder" is the Qur'an. They said this mockingly; had they been certain that the Reminder had been sent down to him, they would not have said, ﴿Indeed, you are mad.﴾ Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: The answer to this verse appears in another surah, in His saying: ﴿You are not, by the favour of your Lord, a madman.﴾ [al-Qalam 68:2]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ Al-Farra' said: "Lawma" and "lawla" are two dialects, both meaning "halla" (why not). Abu ʿUbayda likewise said: they have the same meaning, and he cited Ibn Muqbil:

Lawma al-hayaʾu wa-lawma al-dinu ʿibtukuma
bi-baʿdi ma fikuma idh ʿibtuma ʿawari

Were it not for shame and were it not for religion, I would reproach you both
for some of what is in you, since you have reproached me for my faults.

The exegetes said: They asked for the angels so that they might bear witness to his truthfulness and that God had sent him. God answered them with His saying: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir read "mā tanazzalu" with a open tā' and "al-malāʾikatu" in the nominative. Abu Bakr related from ʿAsim "mā tunazzalu" with a damma on the tā', in the passive voice. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from ʿAsim, and Khalaf read "mā nunazzilu" with a nūn and a shadda on the zāy, and "al-malāʾikata" in the accusative.

Regarding the meaning of "al-haqq" (the truth) there are four opinions:

One: It is the punishment, if they do not believe; this is the view of al-Hasan. The second: It is the message (risala); this is the view of Mujahid. The third: It is the seizing of souls at death; this is the view of Ibn al-Sa'ib. The fourth: It is the Qur'an; this is related by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor would they have been given respite﴾ meaning: the polytheists, ﴿then﴾ i.e., at the time of the descent of the angels, if they had descended.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 15, verse 9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Reminder﴾. It is a custom of kings that when they do something, one of them says, "We did it," meaning himself and his followers. Then this became a habit of the king in his speech, even when he alone performed the action. Thus the Arabs were addressed in the manner of speech that they understand. And al-Dhikr (the Reminder) is the Qur'an, according to the saying of all the exegetes (mufassirun).

Regarding the pronoun in "lahu" (for Him/it), there are two views:

The first: it refers to the Reminder. This is the view of most scholars. Qatadah said: Allah sent it down and then preserved it, so Iblis cannot add falsehood to it or subtract any truth from it.

The second: it refers to the Prophet ﷺ, so the meaning is: ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾ from the devils and the enemies, in response to their saying: ﴿Indeed, you are a madman﴾. This is the saying of Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil.

Allah's saying: ﴿And We certainly sent [messengers] before you﴾, meaning: messengers, so the object was omitted, since the sending (al-irsal) indicates it. And ash-shiya' (the factions/sects): the groups. It is related from al-Farra' that he said: ash-shi'ah is a community that follows one another in whatever matter they agree upon.

Allah's words: ﴿And there never came to them a messenger except that they used to mock him﴾. This is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), and the meaning is: every prophet before you was tested by his people just as you have been tested.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 15, verses 12–13:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Thus do We cause it to enter﴾ (kadhalika naslukuhu). Regarding what is referred to by "thus" there are three opinions:

The first: it is disbelief (al-shirk). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: it is mockery (al-istihza'). This was said by Qatadah.

The third: it is denial (al-takdhib). This was said by Ibn Jurayj and al-Farra'.

The meaning of the verse: just as We caused disbelief to enter the hearts of the factions of the earlier peoples, We cause denial to enter the hearts of these people, so they do not believe. Then He informed about these polytheists, saying: ﴿They do not believe in it﴾. Regarding what is referred to by "it" there are three opinions:

The first: it is the Messenger. The second: it is the Qur'an. The third: it is the punishment.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the example of the earlier peoples has already passed﴾ (wa-qad khalat sunnatu al-awwalin). In this there are two opinions:

One of them: the way of Allah in destroying those who denied has passed on.

The second: their own way of denying the prophets has passed on.

(p-386) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We opened for them a gate from the sky﴾, meaning: the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿and they continued to ascend through it﴾, i.e., they went up. It is said: "ẓalla yafʿalu kadhā" means he did such-and-such during the daytime.

Regarding those referred to by this ascent, there are two opinions:

The first: they are the angels. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Ḍaḥḥāk. The meaning then is: if their eyes were uncovered and they saw an open gate in the sky with the angels ascending through it, they would not have believed in it.

The second: they are the polytheists. This was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatadah. The meaning then is: if We had brought them to the ascent of the sky, they would have perceived nothing but disbelief, due to their obstinacy.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They would surely say, "Our eyes have only been intoxicated."﴾ Most readers recited it with the letter kāf doubled (sukkirat). Ibn Kathir and ʿAbd al-Warith recited it with the letter kāf lightened (sukirat). Al-Farrāʾ said: the meanings of the two readings are close, and the meaning is "was held back," from their saying: "sakarat al-rīḥ" when the wind became calm and still. Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: the meaning of "sukirat" with lightening is taken from the intoxication of wine, meaning that the eyes became bewildered and there occurred in them, through corruption of vision, the same as what occurs to an intoxicated man through a change of the intellect. Ibn al-Anbārī said: if this is so, the meaning of the lightened form is as stated, while "sukkirat" with doubling is used to indicate that this matter occurs repeatedly, time after time. Abū ʿUbayd said: "sukkirat" with doubling is from the "sukur" (dams) that prevent water from flowing, so it is as if these eyes were prevented from seeing, just as a dam prevents water from running. Al-Zajjāj said: "sukkirat" with doubling, the commentators explained it as "were covered," while "sukirat" with lightening means "were bewildered and became still from looking," and the Arabs say "sakirat al-rīḥ yaskaru" when the wind became calm. It was narrated by al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿Our eyes have only been intoxicated﴾ that he said: "Our eyes were seized and confused for us, and we were only bewitched." Mujāhid said: ﴿sukkirat﴾ means "were blocked by magic, so that other than what we see appears to our eyes."

(p-387) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have placed in the sky constellations (buruj)﴾. Regarding the buruj (constellations, or mansions of the sun and moon) there are three opinions.

The first is that they are the mansions (manazil) of the sun and the moon. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Abu Ubayda, along with others. Ibn Qutayba said: Their names are: Aries (al-Hamal), Taurus (al-Thawr), Gemini (al-Jawza'), Cancer (al-Saratan), Leo (al-Asad), Virgo (al-Sunbula), Libra (al-Mizan), Scorpio (al-Aqrab), Sagittarius (al-Qaws), Capricorn (al-Jadi), Aquarius (al-Dalw), and Pisces (al-Hut).

The second is that they are palaces (qusur). This was also related from Ibn Abbas. Ata said: They are palaces in the sky in which there are guards. Ibn Qutayba said: The original meaning of buruj is fortresses (husun).

The third is that they are the stars (kawakib). This was said by Mujahid, Qatada and Muqatil. Abu Salih said: They are the great stars. Qatada said: They were called buruj because of their visibility.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and We adorned it﴾, that is, We made it beautiful with the stars.

Concerning the meaning of al-nazirin (الناظرين, "the observers") there are two opinions: the first is that they are those who see (al-mubsirun); the second is that they are those who take heed (al-mu'tabirun).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We guarded it from every accursed devil (rajim)﴾, that is, We protected it so that no devil could reach it or learn anything of its affairs except by stealth (istiraqan), whereupon a shooting flame pursues him. The word rajim has been explained in (Al 'Imran: 36).

The scholars differed over whether the devils were pelted with the stars before the mission of our Prophet ﷺ or not, on two views:

The first is that they were not pelted until the Prophet ﷺ was sent. This meaning is mentioned in a report (p-388) of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas. It is related in the Two Sahihs, from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out with a group of his companions, intending to go to the market of Ukaz, and the devils had been prevented from receiving news from the sky, and shooting flames were sent against them." The apparent meaning of this hadith is that this did not happen before that. Al-Zajjaj said: What indicates that it only began after the birth of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is that the poets of the Arabs, who used to compare things to lightning and swift things, did not mention falling stars in their poetry. But after the birth of our Prophet ﷺ, the poets began to mention them. Dhu al-Rumma said:

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 15, verse 19–20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the earth — We have spread it out﴾, meaning: We spread it out over the surface of the water. ﴿And We have cast therein firm mountains﴾, which are the fixed mountains (jibal, mountains). ﴿And We have caused to grow therein﴾ — regarding what is referred to by "therein" there are two opinions:

The first: that it is the earth. This was said by most of the scholars. The second: that it is the mountains. This was said by al-Farra'.

(p-391) Regarding His saying: ﴿of every thing weighed (mawzun)﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: that "mawzun" means "known" (ma'lum). This was related by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak also said so. Mujahid and 'Ikrimah, along with others, said: "mawzun" means "measured out" (maqdur). According to this, the meaning is: of a known measure, as if it had been weighed, because the people of this world, when they know the measure of a thing, know it by its weight; so Allah Exalted informed that this thing has a known measure with Him by describing it as "weighed". Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that it proceeds according to a weight of the decree of Allah Exalted, which does not exceed what Allah Exalted has decreed for it, and it is not able to create any increase in it or decrease.

The second: that He meant by it the things that are weighed, such as gold, silver, lead, iron, kohl, and the like. This meaning is related from al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Ibn Zayd and Ibn al-Sa'ib, and al-Farra' chose it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have made for you therein means of livelihood (ma'ayish)﴾ — regarding what is referred to by "therein" and "them" there are two opinions:

The first: that it is the earth.

The second: that it is the things which the earth has caused to grow. "Ma'ayish" is the plural of "ma'isha", and the meaning is: We have made for you therein provisions by which you live.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and those for whom you are not providers﴾ there are four opinions:

The first: that it refers to the beasts and cattle. This was related by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid.

The second: wild animals. This was related by Mansur from Mujahid. Ibn Qutaybah said: the wild beasts, birds, predators, and the like, which the son of Adam does not provide for.

The third: slaves and female slaves. This was said by al-Farra'.

The fourth: slaves, cattle, and beasts. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Al-Farra' said: "man" (من) is in the accusative position, so the meaning is: We have made for you therein the means of livelihood, and the slaves, and the female slaves. It is also said that it is in the genitive position, so the meaning is: We have made for you therein means of livelihood, and for those for whom you are not providers. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: We have made for you the beasts and the slaves, and you have been relieved of the burden of providing for their sustenance.

If it is said: how do you say that "man" here refers to wild animals and beasts, when it is only used for those who have reason?

The answer: when wild animals and others are described with the "ma'ash" (livelihood) which is most commonly described for people, so that it is said of a human that he has a ma'ash, and it is not said of a horse that it has a ma'ash, they were treated as people, as He said: ﴿O ant, enter your dwellings﴾ [al-Naml 18], and He said: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf 4], and He said: ﴿Each in an orbit is swimming﴾ [al-Anbiya' 33]. And if we say that slaves and wild animals are intended by it, then when people and others are combined, people are given precedence over others, due to the excellence of reason and discernment.

Translation:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is not a thing﴾, meaning: there is not any thing ﴿except that with Us are its treasuries﴾. This statement is general, covering everything. However, a group of the exegetes (mufassirun) held that what is meant by it is specifically rain. According to them, the meaning is: there is not any rain except that with Us are its treasuries, i.e., under Our decree and Our management. ﴿And We do not send it down﴾ each year ﴿except in a known measure﴾, neither increasing nor decreasing. So no year has more rain than another, except that Allah, exalted is He, directs it to whomever He wills and withholds it from whomever He wills.

(p-393) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾. Hamzah and Khalaf read "al-rīḥ" (the wind, in the singular). Abu 'Ubaydah held that "lawāqiḥ" (fertilizing) means "malāqiḥ" (fertilizing, in the sense of impregnating), with the mīm dropped from it. The poet said:

"Let Yazid weep, a wretched man, for his humility, and a dishevelled one whom the calamities have tossed about."

He meant "maṭāwiḥ" (those tossed about), and dropped the mīm. So the meaning of the verse according to him is: "And We sent the winds impregnating," and thus the form fā'il here carries the sense of mufʿil, just as fā'il sometimes carries the sense of maf'ūl, as in His saying: ﴿of gushing water﴾ [al-Ṭāriq 6], meaning medfūq (poured forth); and "a pleasing life" [al-Ḥāqqah 21; al-Qāri'ah 7], meaning marḍiyya (pleased with); and as in their saying: "a sleeping night" (laylun nā'im), meaning one in which there is sleeping (manūm fīhi); and they say: "the plant has become green" (abqala al-nabt), so it is bāqil, meaning mubqil (verdant).

Ibn Qutaybah said: Abu 'Ubaydah intends that they fertilize the trees and fertilize the clouds, as if they bring them forth. I do not know what compelled him to this interpretation, with such strain, when he finds the Arabs calling the winds "lawāqiḥ" and the wind "lāqiḥ." Al-Ṭirimmāh said, describing a cloak he had spread over his companions in the sun, who sheltered beneath it:

"Restless among the branches of the wind, for a fertilizing one among them and a barren one."

So "lāqiḥ" is the south wind, and "ḥā'il" (barren) is the north wind. They also call the north wind "ʿaqīm" (barren), and "ʿaqīm" is that which bears no fruit, just as they named the south wind "lāqiḥ." Kuthayyir said:

"And there passed over the coarse dust, its barren one (ʿaqīmuhā)."

He means the north wind. They called the wind "lāqiḥ," that is, bearing (ḥāmil), because it carries the clouds (p-394) and turns them, directs them, then dissolves them so that they fall as rain. On this view it is a bearer, and this is supported by His saying: ﴿until, when they bear a heavy cloud﴾ [al-A'rāf 57], meaning they carried. Ibn al-Anbārī said: The wind's carrying of water and other things is compared to the pregnancy the she-camel carries in her womb. Likewise they say "a war is pregnant" (ḥarbun lāqiḥ), because of the evil it contains. So according to Abu 'Ubaydah's view, the meaning of "lawāqiḥ" is that they impregnate other things; and according to Ibn Qutaybah's view, that they become pregnant themselves. Most of the ḥadīths indicate the first view.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd said: God sends the winds to impregnate the clouds, so they bear water, then they squeeze it out and then stir it, and it flows as the milch-camel flows. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: God sends the winds upon the clouds, and they impregnate them, so they become full of water. Al-Nakha'ī said: They impregnate the clouds but do not impregnate the trees. Al-Ḥasan, among others, said: They impregnate both the clouds and the trees, meaning that they impregnate the clouds until they rain, and the trees until they bear fruit.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We sent down water from the sky﴾, meaning from the clouds, ﴿water﴾, meaning rain, ﴿and gave it to you to drink﴾, meaning We made it a drink for you. Al-Farrā' said: The Arabs agree that they say "saqaytu al-rajul, fa-anā asqīhi" (I gave the man to drink) when you give him drink to his lips; but when they make a river for a man they say "asqaytuhu" and "saqaytuhu," and likewise the watering from rain (al-suqyā min al-ghayth), for which they say "saqaytu" and "asqaytu." Abu 'Ubaydah said: Whatever comes from the sky has two forms: "asqāhu Allāh" and "saqāhu Allāh." Labīd said:

"He gave drink to my people, the Banū Majd, and gave drink to Numayr and the tribes of Hilāl."

So he used both forms. And you say: "saqaytu al-rajul māʾan wa-sharāban min laban wa-ghayrihi" (I gave the man water and drink of milk and other things), and there is only one form for this, without an alif, when it is at the lips; but when you make a drinking-place for him, it is "asqaytuhu," and "asqaytu arḍahu" (I watered his land), and "wa-ibilahu" (his camels), and it cannot be otherwise. Likewise when you ask drink for him, as the saying of Dhū al-Rummah:

"I halted at the traces of Miyya, my she-camel, and I did not cease weeping there and addressing it."

"And I gave it drink until, from what I pour out, its stones and its hollows nearly spoke to me."

So when you give him a skin to make into a water-skin, you have "asqaytuhu iyyāhu" (I gave it to him to drink).

Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two opinions:

(p-396) The first: "A beautiful woman used to pray behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so some of the people would move forward until they were in the first row, so that they would not see her, and some would hold back until they were in the last row. The first: the advancing is to the first row and the delaying is away from it. This accords with the two reported occasions of revelation. The fifth: those who precede are those who go forward in good, and those who delay are those who hinder from it. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The sixth: those who precede are in the ranks of battle, and those who hold back from them. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The seventh: those who precede are those who were killed in jihad, and those who delay are those who were not killed. This was said by al-Qurazi.

The eighth: those who precede are the first of creation, and those who delay are the last of creation. This was said by al-Sha'bi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 15, verse 26–29:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We created man﴾, meaning Adam, ﴿from clay of sounding dry mud﴾ (ṣalṣāl). There are three opinions concerning it:

The first: it is dry clay that has not been touched by fire; when you tap it, it rings, and you hear a sound from it. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, Abu ʿUbayda and Ibn Qutayba.

The second: it is stinking clay. This was said by Mujahid, al-Kisa'i and Abu ʿUbayd. It is said: ṣalla al-laḥm (the meat became putrid), when its smell changed.

The third: it is clay mixed with sand, so that it makes a sound when struck. This was said by al-Farra'.

As for ḥamaʾ (black mud), Abu ʿUbayda said: it is the plural of ḥamʾah, which is clay that has changed. Ibn al-Anbari said: there is no disagreement that ḥamaʾ is black clay whose smell has changed. al-Suddi narrated from his shaykhs, saying: the earth was moistened until it became clay, then it was left until it became foul and changed.

The first: it also means stinking. This was narrated by Mujahid from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid and Qatada, among others, said so. Ibn Qutayba said: al-masnūn means that whose smell has changed.

The second: it is moist clay. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: it is poured out. This was said by Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' and Abu ʿUbayd.

The fourth: it is scraped/rubbed. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. Whoever says it is poured out, relies on the saying of the Arabs: qad sanantu ʿalayya al-māʾ, meaning when you poured water over me. "It shows you the sunna (form) of a face, unblemished, smooth, with no mole or scar upon it."

Whoever says it is scraped, relies on the saying of the Arabs: sanantu al-ḥajar ʿalā al-ḥajar, meaning when you rub one stone against another. The third: he is Iblis. This was said by al-Hasan, ʿAta', Qatada and Muqatil.

If it is said: Is not the father of the jinn Iblis? There are two answers to this:

One of them: he is him, so this opinion is the same as the one before it.

The second: al-Jann is the father of the jinn, and Iblis is the father of the shayatin, so there is a difference between them according to what we have mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas. The scholars said: he was named jann because he is concealed from the eyes.

Regarding the meaning of "authority" (sultan), there are two opinions:

The first is that it means proof or argument, as said by Ibn Jarir, so the meaning is: you have no argument for misleading them.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna was asked about this verse and said: "You have no authority over them to cast them into a sin for which My forgiveness would be too narrow."

His words, ﴿It has seven gates﴾, mean that its levels are one above another. Ibn Jarir said: "It has seven gates. The first is Jahannam, then Laza, then al-Hutama, then al-Sa'ir, then Saqar, then al-Jahim, then al-Hawiyah." Al-Dahhak said: "They are seven stages, one above another. The highest of them contains the people of tawhid (monotheism; the affirmation of God's oneness), who are punished according to the measure of their sins and then leave. **The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 15, verses 45–48:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing (muttaqin) will be in gardens and springs﴾. We have already explained the meaning of *taqwa* (God-consciousness, piety) and of the gardens (*jannat*) in (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:2 and 25). As for the springs, they are springs of water, wine, *salsabil*, *tasnim*, and others, including what is mentioned as being among the drinks of Paradise.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Enter them in peace﴾. The meaning is: it will be said to them, "Enter them in peace." There are three opinions regarding this:

The first: in safety from the Fire. The second: in safety from every calamity. The third: with a greeting from Allah.

Regarding His saying ﴿secure﴾, there are four opinions:

The first: secure from the punishment of Allah. The second: from leaving (Paradise). The third: from death. The fourth: from fear and sickness.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We will remove whatever rancor is in their breasts﴾. We have already mentioned its interpretation in Surah (p. 404) (al-A'raf, 43), for the exegetes have mentioned here what was mentioned there, both in interpretation and in the occasion of revelation.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿as brothers﴾. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), and the meaning is that they will be mutually affectionate.

If it is asked: how is "brothers" in the accusative as a state, which implies that brotherhood occurred together with the removal of rancor, when brotherhood among them already existed in this world?

Ibn al-Anbari has answered this, saying: the brotherhood that passed in this world was mixed with grudges and enmity, whereas this brotherhood among them that exists when rancor is removed is the brotherhood of purity and sincerity. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative as a form of praise; the meaning being: "Mention brothers."

As for ﴿thrones﴾ (*surur*), it is the plural of *sarir*. Ibn Abbas said: "on thrones of gold adorned with chrysolite, pearls, and rubies; the throne is as far as the distance between Aden and Ayla." ﴿Facing one another﴾: none of them sees the back of another; wherever he turns, he sees a face he loves facing him.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿No fatigue will touch them therein﴾. That is: no exhaustion or weariness will afflict them in Paradise.

Allah's saying: ﴿of a knowing boy﴾, meaning: he will reach maturity and will have knowledge.

(p-406) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Do you give me good tidings, though old age has touched me?"﴾ That is, of a child, ﴿though old age has touched me﴾, that is, in a state of old age and decrepitude. ﴿So what is it that you announce?﴾ Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "tubashshirun" with an open nun (fatḥ). Nafi' read it with a kasra on the nun, and Ibn Kathir agreed with him in the kasra but doubled the shin (tashdid). This is an interrogative of wonder, as if he were amazed at having a child in his old age. ﴿They said, "We give you good tidings in truth"﴾, that is, with what Allah has decreed will happen, ﴿so do not be of those who despair﴾, meaning those who lose hope.

﴿He said, "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord, except the astray?"﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read "yaqnaṭu" with an open nun throughout the Qur'an. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "yaqnitu" with a kasra on the nun. All of them read ﴿after they had despaired﴾ [al-Shura: 28] with an open nun. Kharijah narrated from Abu 'Amr "yaqnuṭu" with a damma on the nun. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said "qanita yaqnatu" and "qanata yaqnitu," and al-qunut means despair (al-yas). Ibrahim was not one who despaired, but he considered the existence of a child unlikely.

﴿He said, "What then is your business?"﴾ That is, what is your matter? ﴿They said, "We have been sent"﴾, that is, with punishment. As for His saying: ﴿except the family of Lut﴾, it is an exception not belonging to the first part. The family of Lut are his believing followers.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We will deliver them﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "lamunajjuhum" with a doubled jim. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "lamunjuhum" with a single jim.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except his wife﴾. The meaning: Indeed We will deliver them, except his wife. ﴿We have decreed﴾. Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim "qadarna" with a light qaf. The meaning is one: it is said qaddarta and qadarta, and the meaning is: We have decided. ﴿Indeed, she is among those who remain behind﴾, meaning those who remain in punishment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 15, verse 72–77:

(p-408) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿By your life﴾ has three opinions:

The first: its meaning is: "By your life, O Muhammad." Abu al-Jawza' narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "By your livelihood (la'aysuka)." Ibn Abi Talha narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Akhfash said the same, and it goes back to the meaning of the first.

The third: its meaning is: "By your right over your community." The Arabs say: "La'amru Allah, I will not stand," meaning: "By the right of God." Ibn al-Anbari mentioned it. He said: "In al-'amr there are three dialects: 'amr, 'umr and 'umur, and among the Arabs it means survival (al-baqa')." Al-Zajjaj related that al-Khalil, Sibawayh and all the people of the language said: "al-'amr and al-'umr have one meaning. When it is used in an oath, it is pronounced only with a fatha." They preferred the fatha in the oath because the fatha is lighter for them, and they emphasize oaths with "la'amri" and "la'amruka." When their use of it became frequent, they adhered to the lighter form. He said: The grammarians said: "la'amruka" is in the nominative by way of the inceptive (al-ibtida'), and the predicate is omitted, and the meaning is: "By your life is my oath," and "By your life is that by which I swear," and the predicate was omitted because the speech contains an indication of it. The meaning: I swear ﴿that they, in their intoxication, are wandering blindly﴾.

Regarding the meaning of this "intoxication" (sakra) there are two opinions:

One: that it means misguidance, said by Qatada.

The second: that it means heedlessness, said by al-A'mash. We have explained the meaning of 'amah (blind wandering) in the surah of al-Baqara (2:15). Regarding those referred to by "these," there are two opinions: One: that they are the people of Lut, said by most of the scholars. The second: that they are the people of our Prophet (ﷺ), said by 'Ata'.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So the shout seized them﴾, meaning: the shout of punishment, and it was the shout of Jibril (peace be upon him). ﴿At sunrise﴾ — al-Zajjaj said: It is said: "Ashraqna," so we are "mushriqun," when they encounter the sunrise, which is its rising, just as it is said "asbahna" when they encounter the morning. It is said: "sharaqat al-shams" when the sun rose, and "ashraqat" when it shone and became clear. This is the most common usage in the language. It has been said that sharaqat and ashraqat have one meaning, except that "mushriqin" means encountering the rising of the sun.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So We made its highest part its lowest﴾ — we have explained this verse in the surah of Hud (11:82).

Regarding "those who discern" (al-mutawassimin) there are four opinions:

The first: that they are those who perceive insight (al-mutafarrisun). Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Beware of the insight of the believer, for he looks with the light of God," then he recited: "Indeed in that are signs for those who discern (al-mutawassimin)." He said: the mutafarrisin. This is also the view of Mujahid and Ibn Qutayba. Ibn Qutayba said: It is said: "Tawassamtu fi fulan al-khayr," meaning: I clearly recognized it. Al-Zajjaj said: al-mutawassimun, in the language, are the observers who are careful in their looking until they know the reality of the mark of a thing. It is said: "Tawassamtu fi fulan kadha," meaning: I recognized the mark of that in him. Others said: al-mutawassim is the one who looks at the sign that indicates a thing. The second: those who take lesson (al-mu'tabirun), said by Qatada. The third: those who look (al-nazirun), said by al-Dahhak. The fourth: those who reflect (al-mutafakkirun), said by Ibn Zayd and al-Farra'.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed it﴾, meaning: the town of the people of Lut, ﴿is on a road that remains﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

One: that it is on a clear road, narrated by Nahshal from al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and said by Qatada and al-Zajjaj. Ibn Zayd said: on a manifest road.

The second: that it is on destruction. Abu Rawq narrated it from al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and the meaning is: in its state of destruction it has not been resettled until now, so reflection upon it is possible, and it lies on the road of Quraysh when they travel to Syria.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 15, verses 87–89:**

Allah's words, ﴿And We have given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾. The occasion of its revelation was that seven caravans arrived from Busra and Adhri'at, belonging to the Jews of Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir, all on one day. They carried various kinds of cloth, perfume and jewels. The Muslims said, "If these possessions were ours, we would strengthen ourselves with them and spend them in the way of Allah." So Allah revealed this verse and said, "I have given you seven verses, which are better for you than these seven caravans." What confirms this is His words, ﴿Do not extend your eyes…﴾ and the verse that follows. This was related by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl.

[p. 413] Regarding the meaning of "the seven oft-repeated," there are four opinions:

The first: it is the Opening of the Book (al-Fatiha). This was said by Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Mas'ud in one report, Ibn Abbas in the report of most of those who narrated from him, Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr in one report, Mujahid in one report, Ata, Qatada, and others. According to this view, it is called "seven" because it has seven verses.

As for why it is called "oft-repeated (al-mathani)," there are seven opinions:

One: because Allah set it apart for the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ and did not give it to any nation before them. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas.

The second: because it is recited twice in every rak'a. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is, "We gave you the seven verses that are repeated in every rak'a." The particle "min" (from) entered for emphasis, as in His words, ﴿And for them therein are of all the fruits﴾ [Muhammad 47:15]. Ibn Qutayba said: al-Hamd (the Opening) was called "mathani" because it is recited in every prayer.

The third: because it is that by which Allah is praised, since it contains the praise of Allah, His Oneness, and mention of His dominion. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: because it contains "the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful" twice. This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi from some linguists, and this is based on the view of those who consider the basmala to be part of it.

The fifth: because it is divided between Allah the Exalted and His servant. This is supported by the hadith of Abu Hurayra: "I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant."

The sixth: (p. 414) because it was revealed twice. This was mentioned by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl.

The seventh: because its words are repeated, such as: al-Rahman al-Rahim; iyyaka iyyaka; al-sirat sirat; alayhim alayhim; ghayr ghayr. This was mentioned by some exegetes (mufassirun). Among its greatest virtues is that Allah placed it in one section, and the entire Qur'an in another section, and He bestowed it as a favour just as He bestowed the entire Qur'an as a favour.

The second opinion: they are the seven long [surahs] (al-sab' al-tiwal). This was said by Ibn Mas'ud in one report, Ibn Abbas in one report, Sa'id ibn Jubayr in one report, Mujahid in one report, and al-Dahhak. The seven long surahs are: al-Baqara, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'ida, al-An'am, al-A'raf, and for the seventh there are three opinions: one, that it is Yunus, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr; two, that it is Bara'a (al-Tawba), said by Abu Malik; three, that it is both al-Anfal and Bara'a together, narrated by Sufyan from Mis'ar from some people of knowledge. Ibn Qutayba said: they used to regard al-Anfal and Bara'a as one surah, and for that reason they did not separate them. Shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi said: [the seven] are the long ones, and do not pronounce it with a kasra.

According to this view, there are two opinions regarding why they are called "oft-repeated": one, because the limits (hudud), obligations (fara'id) and parables (amthal) are repeated in them; this was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: because they go beyond the first hundred [verses] into the second hundred; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The third opinion: the seven oft-repeated are seven meanings revealed in the Qur'an: command, prohibition, glad tidings, warning, the striking of parables, the enumeration of blessings, and the reports of past nations. This was said by Ziyad ibn Abi Maryam.

The fourth opinion: the oft-repeated is the entire Qur'an. This was said by Tawus, al-Dahhak, and Abu Malik. According to this view, there are four opinions regarding why the Qur'an is called "oft-repeated":

Its root meaning is splitting and opening, as if to say: split falsehood with your truth. Al-Zajjaj said: Make manifest what you are commanded with, taken from al-sadi' (the dawn), which is the morning, as the poet said:

"As if the whiteness of his blaze were the dawn."

Al-Farra' said: He did not say "what you are commanded with" (bihi) because he intended: proclaim the matter openly. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned that "with it" (bihi) is implied, as you would say: "I passed by the one you passed by."

Third: What is meant is loudly reciting the Qur'an in prayer. Ibn Abi Najih related it from Mujahid. Musa ibn 'Ubayda said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained hidden until this verse was revealed, and then he and his companions went out."

Regarding His saying: ﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾, there are three interpretations:

First: Refrain from fighting them.

(p-421) Second: Do not care about them, and do not heed their blame for making your affair manifest.

Third: Turn away from concern over their mockery. Most exegetes hold that this part of the verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword (the verse of the sword, Q 9:5).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 15, verse 95–99:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have sufficed you against the mockers﴾. The meaning: so proclaim My command as I have sufficed you against the mockers. They were a people who used to mock him and the Qur'an. Concerning their number there are two statements:

The first: they were five: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Zam'a, al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth, al-As ibn Wa'il, and al-Harith ibn Qays. This was said by Ibn Abbas. The name of Abu Zam'a was al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib. Likewise Sa'id ibn Jubayr mentioned them, except that in place of al-Harith ibn Qays he said al-Harith ibn Ghaytala. al-Zuhri said: Ghaytala was his mother and Qays was his father, so he is one person. I have only mentioned this so that it is not assumed he is someone else. I have mentioned in the book "al-Talqih" those among the Companions, the Successors and those after them who are ascribed to their mothers, and I have named their fathers so that it may be known to which of the two parents they are ascribed. In a narration from Ibn Abbas, in place of al-Harith ibn Qays, it is: Adi ibn Qays.

The second: they were seven. This was said by al-Sha'bi and Ibn Abi Bazza. Ibn Abi Bazza counted them, saying: al-As ibn Wa'il, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-Harith ibn Adi, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth, and Asram and Bu'kuk, the two sons of Abd al-Harith ibn al-Sabbaq. (p-422) Likewise Muqatil counted them, except that in place of al-Harith ibn Adi he said: al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi, and he said: Asram and Bu'kuk, the two sons of al-Hajjaj ibn al-Sabbaq.

Mention of what Allah destroyed them with, and what He sufficed His Messenger ﷺ regarding their affair.

The exegetes said: "Jibril came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while the mockers were circumambulating the House, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira passed by. Jibril said: 'O Muhammad, how do you find this?' He said: 'Wretched is the servant of Allah.' He said: 'You have been sufficed,' and he pointed to al-Walid's shin. Then al-Walid passed by a man fletching an arrow for himself, and a splinter of an arrow caught on his waistwrap. Pride prevented him from bending down to remove it, and it began to strike his shin. He fell ill and died. It was also said: an arrow caught on his garment and struck his cubital artery, cutting it, and he died. Al-As ibn Wa'il passed by, and Jibril said: 'How do you find this, O Muhammad?' He said: 'Wretched is the servant of Allah.' He pointed to the sole of his foot and said: 'You have been sufficed.' A thorn entered the sole of his foot, his foot swelled, and he died. Al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib passed by, and he said: 'How do you find this?' He said: 'A wretched servant.' He pointed with his hand to his eyes, and he became blind and perished. It was also said: he began to butt his head against the trees and strike his face with thorns, and he cried out to his servant, who said: 'I see no one doing this to you except yourself.' He died saying: 'The Lord of Muhammad has killed me.' Al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth passed by, and Jibril said: 'How do you find this?' He said: 'Wretched is the servant of Allah.' He said: 'You have been sufficed,' and he pointed to his belly. His belly swelled up and he died. It was also said: a thorn struck his eye and his pupils ran out. It was also said: he went out from his family and the simoom struck him, and he turned black until he became like an Abyssinian; when he came to his family they did not recognize him, and they closed the doors against him until he died. (p-423) Al-Harith ibn Qays passed by him, and he said: 'How do you find this?' He said: 'A wretched servant.' He pointed to his head and said: 'You have been sufficed.' His head swelled and he died. It was also said: he was struck by thirst, and he kept drinking water until his belly burst. As for Asram and Bu'kuk, Muqatil said: one of them was struck by the dubayla (a boil) and the other by pleurisy, and both died." Ikrima said: the mockers perished before Badr. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: they were all destroyed in one day and night.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We know that your breast becomes constricted by what they say﴾. Concerning it there are two statements:

The first: it is denial. The second: it is mockery.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise﴾. Concerning it there are two statements:

The first: say: "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," said by al-Dahhak. The second: pray by the command of your Lord, said by Muqatil.

Concerning His saying: ﴿And be among those who prostrate﴾ there are two statements:

The first: among those who pray. The second: among those who are humble. Both were related from Ibn Abbas.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Until there comes to you the certainty﴾. Concerning it there are two statements:

The first: that it is death. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and the majority. It was called "certainty" because it is certain to occur. al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: worship your Lord forever. Had it been said "worship your Lord" without a time limit, it would have been permissible for a person who worshipped once to be obedient; but when He said "until there comes to you the certainty," he was commanded to persist in worship as long as he lived.
